articles.title: One killed, several injured in sword attack at Swedish school
articles.summary: An 18-year-old man armed with a sword attacked students at a Swedish high school on Friday, killing one person and injuring three, and police shot and detained him as media reported the attacker was a former student at the school.
articles.body: An 18-year-old man armed with a sword attacked students at a Swedish high school on Friday, killing one person and injuring three, and police shot and detained him as media reported the attacker was a former student at the school. The incident occurred on Friday afternoon at the Brinell high school in the central Swedish town of Fagersta, which has about 13,000 residents. The school had just reopened after summer recess, and for some students, it was their first day. Police told a press conference that the suspect was an 18-year-old man whom they shot and took into custody on suspicion of murder. Local police chief Tommy Alriksson said officers responded quickly to the school, which has 450 students ages 16 to 20. “The first patrol entered and let us know that the perpetrator was subdued with gunfire,” he said. Public broadcaster SVT, citing unnamed sources, reported the attacker, wearing a helmet and carrying a sword, was a former student at the school with a previous conviction for assault. The local health authority said two victims were teenage boys who were severely injured. A third injured person was released from hospital. ‘First it was just a regular day’ “First it was just a regular day really. But then … I saw a guy all covered in blood, at least down his back anyway. Then I saw the police and they flooded in,” one Brinell student, Nellie, told Reuters alongside her mother Agnes Strandberg after a five-hour lockdown at the school. Another student, Abdulrahem Salmo, said he had seen a victim with a bloody stab wound in the arm. “Then people called the police and we just all ran from there because we were afraid,” he told SVT. Several other schools and public buildings in Fagersta were also initially locked down. Fagersta Mayor Asa-Marta Sjostrom said the small town was shaken. “Our and the school’s main focus right now is to take care of our students and our employees,” she told reporters. “We are working together … to create safety and provide support to those who need it.” Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson cancelled a speech he was due to hold on Saturday, news agency TT reported. “Our thoughts are with all those affected,” he wrote in a post on social media platform X. Sweden’s King Carl XVI Gustaf said in the statement released by the royal household that he received news of the attack “with dismay and sadness.” Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson, whose center-left coalition leads opinion polls for next month’s parliamentary election, said: “All of Sweden stands together with Fagersta at this difficult time.” Previous attacks According to the Aftonbladet daily, police were investigating a TikTok account in connection with Friday’s violence that posted a picture of a sword 20 minutes before the attack. Dagens Nyheter newspaper said the picture appeared to be taken in a restroom at the school based on details in the background. Before the month-old account was taken down on Friday, it contained videos that referred to two episodes of mass violence in Sweden along with Norwegian far-right mass murderer Anders Behring Breivik. Sweden’s worst mass shooting occurred in February 2025 at a school in the south-central city of Orebro, when a gunman killed 10 people before turning the weapon on himself. In 2015, a masked swordsman killed a teaching assistant and two boys at a school in Trollhattan, western Sweden, before being shot dead by police, who later said the attack was racially motivated.

articles.title: Quiet on set. How AI transformed China’s microdrama scene
articles.summary: The breakneck AI transformation of the industry is the kind of technological disruption that many creatives fear could upend movie-making far beyond China.
articles.body: Everything seemed to be business as usual as filming got underway on a dimly lit set in a basement in Hengdian, a town nicknamed “China’s Hollywood” for its sprawling complex of film studios. Cameramen raced around hectically setting up lights and checking shots as choreographers ran through fight sequences and a prop team worked out how to hoist a net that would later restrain a hostage. Actors, most dressed as assassins and hitmen, milled about or squatted, smoking cigarettes and getting occasional touch-ups from roving hair stylists and make-up artists as they waited for their scene to start. But behind the bustle was a new reality: while just a few months ago, production of these so-called “microdramas” was flourishing in Hengdian and other hubs – today, these sets are falling quiet. Seemingly overnight, new AI-video generation tools have taken over the microdrama industry, able to produce these popular, vertical shows at a fraction of the cost, decimating the number of live-action productions across the country and flooding platforms with AI-made content. More than 120,000 microdramas were released in the first three months of this year — with 95% of those generated by AI, according to Chinese state media. That’s made the industry one of the most visible examples of how China’s breakneck AI transformation is impacting people’s livelihoods — wiping out jobs and creating new ones, leaving everyone unsure what’s next. It’s the kind of technological disruption that many creatives fear could upend movie-making far beyond China. Between takes actor Junlin, who asked to be identified by her stage name, talks about how she’s struggling to stay afloat as a “bitter winter” has arrived for productions like hers. “With fewer productions hiring, your space for survival is constantly squeezed,” said the 24-year-old, dressed in combat boots and a high ponytail to play a head assassin who storms around with a posse of hitmen in an upcoming microdrama. She’d worked only seven days in June, a sharp fall from the spring when she’d been filming 25 out of about 30 days per month in Hengdian and other cities. “I’m someone who gets anxious easily,” she said. “If I’m not on set, I would be in a constant state of anxiety.” Boom time Hengdian, a town of just over 200,000 tucked in a rural part of eastern China’s Zhejiang province, had been booming with the rise of the microdrama industry in recent years. Broken into roughly 90-second episodes, microdramas first emerged during the pandemic, capitalizing on the popularity of short video apps like Douyin and Kuaishou as cinemas and studios closed. While each episode is designed to be quick to consume on a mobile phone, together the clips weave together plotlines that can stretch the length of a feature film. These microdramas — and their often soapy or outlandish plots about wicked mother-in-laws, mistaken identities, wartime heroics and wronged lovers — have since proliferated in China and spread to audiences overseas, where they’ve spawned a fast-growing, multi-billion-dollar industry. They’ve also caught the attention of China’s censors, who are tightening oversight of microdramas with new rules set to take effect in September. Plotlines, for example, will need to “adhere to correct political direction.” Last year, the domestic microdrama industry was valued at nearly $15 billion, according to market research firm DataEye, almost double the market size for box-office feature films in the country. Its rise ushered in a welcome heyday for young creatives at a time of high youth unemployment in China. “Once microdramas took off, there was a nonstop stream of roles I could take on as long as I wanted to film,” said Bi Zhiqiang, 27, another actor living in Hengdian, who quickly built a career after moving there in 2021 as the industry was taking shape. “Many people who didn’t even study acting or film and television joined because there were more and more opportunities.” The lure drew thousands of crews to Hengdian last year to shoot projects in and around the sprawling Hengdian World Studios. It was a fresh injection of energy for the town and its decades-old eponymous studio, known for its large-scale replicas of some of China’s iconic imperial architecture, like the Summer Palace and the Forbidden City, and for birthing Chinese blockbusters. Other hubs — like Qingdao, Xi’an, and Zhengzhou — emerged across the country, too, with microdrama crews shooting in expressly built complexes with fake mansions, boardrooms, and ERs. But the industry quickly became a pressure cooker for actors and production crews, due to a hyper-competitive model built around cranking out as many microdramas as possible in the hopes that one would go viral. Actors and crew describe standard 18 to 20-hour working days as productions rushed to stay within budget while shooting what are essentially feature-length movies in the space of roughly a week. “As long as they keep filming, they can keep releasing. And the logic is — there will always be one that becomes a hit,” said Guo Ertai, a director and actor at the National Theater of China in Beijing, who followed audiences and money into the microdrama industry several years ago. At the bottom of the pecking order are extras, who might work long shifts for as little as 10 Chinese yuan ($1.50) per hour, a wage one former actor commented wryly was less than the rental rate for some of the animals used in productions. Even still, the allure of success kept the industry flush with young, ambitious actors, directors and creatives. Unlike film, which has a high barrier to entry, microdramas “gave an ordinary person an opportunity,” said Guo, the director. The thinking is “‘I can become rich overnight, I can become a star overnight, I can earn a lot of money overnight with very little outlay,’” he said. Microdrama actors have become celebrities in their own right with millions of followers on social media platforms. Some television and film stars — including martial arts legend Jet Li — have starred in microdramas. Even those without broad name recognition, who were able to land leading roles in successful dramas, could make multiples of an average monthly urban wage. But as more money and bigger names entered, competition grew fiercer, pushing a drive to export the dramas overseas for more revenue — and use whatever means available to cut costs. Enter AI It took a few weeks for actor Zhuang Wenjie, 28, to realize something was wrong when she returned to Hengdian after celebrating the Chinese New Year holiday in her hometown in February. She had moved to the area last summer and felt she was just beginning to make a name for herself and could start auditioning for higher profile roles. At first, she didn’t quite connect the empty streets around her with the growing number of AI-generated microdramas she saw on her social media feeds. Soon, though, it became obvious: people weren’t returning because jobs had dried up. “Suddenly (there was) a feeling of impending crisis,” Zhuang said. ByteDance’s SeeDance 2.0 had arrived. Seemingly overnight, Chinese social media was swamped with realistic-looking, AI-generated videos, as users played around with the new, powerful video generation tool. And when it came to microdramas, SeeDance 2.0 was well positioned. ByteDance owns two of the main platforms in China that host microdramas: Douyin, Tiktok’s sister app, and Hongguo. It also has a repository of novels that make up a well of copyrighted material for scripts that collaborating production teams can draw from. Other tech firms have released rival video-generating technology in recent months, including another short video app owner Kuaishuo, tech giant Alibaba and AI firm MiniMax. Using next-gen AI video tools, a 120-minute project of ordinary quality can take a five-member team roughly a week to produce and cost some 15,000 yuan, about $2,200, one production firm told CNN — less than a tenth of what’s typically cited as the low-end cost of a live production. In the first half of the year on Douyin alone, 220,000 new AI-generated microdramas racked up a staggering 500 billion views, according to DataEye, the market research firm. Some were animations, but more than half since March used AI that simulated real people. Zhuang decided to leave town in April, joining an exodus of actors and crew from the area. “The number of jobs in Hengdian was decreasing day by day, and the pay was also getting lower and lower every day … the hardship really did defeat me,” she said. Actors who did stay on described cratering salaries, such as being offered 300 yuan (about $45) a day to play the kind of leading role that would have previously paid thousands. Some have turned to side jobs to make ends meet. Liu Yuzhan, 29, says he’d been making steady money booking four new roles a month in the past couple years. Now, Liu says he’s picking up extra work as a food delivery driver. “I have my own mortgage and I’m responsible for my parents’ retirement. Given the current market of microdramas… it’s simply not enough to cover my daily expenses,” he said. And a new crop of companies, editors and entrepreneurs have poured into the space. Among them is Tan Chen, a 21-year-old college student who founded a startup that began focusing on AI production in April. His team, which is based in Jinan, a provincial capital in eastern China, takes scripts or novels, and “optimizes” them for microdramas by crunching down the narratives and ramping up the excitement and suspense. Employees known as “card-pullers” must use prompts — typically written with the help of AI — to repeatedly generate AI video clips until they get ones that best convey the scene, which are then edited together. But just like actors and live production crews, these creatives are also feeling the squeeze. A crush of programmers joined the industry and middlemen taking a cut to link creators with clients have multiplied, driving down profits for teams like Tan’s. He’s now fielding projects for as low as 150 yuan per minute — around $20. “This rapidly growing market inevitably has a certain degree of bubble,” he said. His company also recently switched to making AI-generated cartoons to avoid inadvertently using AI images that draw from real actor’s faces. ‘If you can’t beat it’ The use of AI characters that resemble real-life actors, without permission, has become a key issue in the industry — with at least one case of a well-known actor receiving court-ordered compensation, state media reports. But other actors, aren’t so lucky. Actor Yu Shutian, 31, recently found what she believes was her own face “blended into AI,” after fans alerted her to an AI-generated character that resembled her. She knew it was nearly impossible to prove the likeness was based on her face, so she never pursued legal action. She also says she realized it was probably the technology, not the creator who was responsible. “AI is unstoppable. If you can’t beat it, join it, so I’d rather find a reasonable way to embrace AI,” said Yu, who is starting to use the tech as she’s moved some of her focus to directing. That sentiment illustrates a central tension raised by many of the actors who shared their stories with CNN. While AI may render the miles of studio space and life-sized sets of places like Hengdian unnecessary, what role humans — including actors — ultimately play in the industry, working alongside AI to create art and entertainment, is far from settled, they say. Microdrama streaming app Hongguo in recent weeks raised production standards around AI-generated dramas, and ratings in recent weeks suggest there’s still viewer appetite for “real people dramas,” which rank in the platform’s top 10 alongside AI productions and cartoons. “AI is formulaic — it can’t express the full range of human emotions and desires,” said Junlin, the actor who is staying put, for now, in Hengdian. “How could it possibly replace humans?” But when it comes to the transformation underway in her industry, she sees the newer actors like herself, who are still trying to make it, as the most vulnerable. “AI absolutely can’t replace a real person,” she said. “But it might be able to replace me.”

Cameramen raced around hectically setting up lights and checking shots as choreographers ran through fight sequences and a prop team worked out how to hoist a net that would later restrain a hostage. Actors, most dressed as assassins and hitmen, milled about or squatted, smoking cigarettes and getting occasional touch-ups from roving hair stylists and make-up artists as they waited for their scene to start. It’s the kind of technological disruption that many creatives fear could upend movie-making far beyond China. Unlike film, which has a high barrier to entry, microdramas “gave an ordinary person an opportunity,” said Guo, the director. The thinking is “‘I can become rich overnight, I can become a star overnight, I can earn a lot of money overnight with very little outlay,’” he said. articles.title: Spain’s ‘wolf boy of Sierra Morena’ dies aged 80
articles.summary: For most of his childhood, Marcos Rodríguez Pantoja lived in remote Spanish mountains, isolated from human contact. He spent 12 extraordinary years being raised by wolves, after early tragedy had led to his abandonment.
articles.body: He became known as “the wolf boy of Sierra Morena.” For most of his childhood, Marcos Rodríguez Pantoja lived in these remote Spanish mountains, isolated from human contact. He spent 12 extraordinary years being raised by wolves, after early tragedy had led to his abandonment. Rodríguez eventually returned to civilization and settled in the hamlet of Rante in 2001, where he lived until his death last week, aged 80, according to the local government of San Cibrao das Viñas. “He was a person made of earth, wind, air, rain, and hunting dens,” Arturo Arcones, who knew Rodríguez in his final years, told Spain’s public broadcaster RTVE. “He always said that his happiest life was with the wolves, because he didn’t feel very comfortable with humans.” Born in 1946, in a country recovering from a civil war and a world war, Rodríguez entered a life marked by poverty in the southern Spanish village of Añora. After his mother’s death, Rodríguez’s siblings went to live with relatives while he stayed with his father, who remarried and moved the family to the Sierra Morena mountains to make charcoal, according to Professor Gabriel Janer Manila. As part of a social study, Manila spent five months interviewing Rodríguez for the philosophy department at the University of Palma de Mallorca. Pantoja was abused by his stepmother and was sold by his father to an elderly goat herder when he was just seven, public broadcaster RTVE reported. “They took me to the mountains, to a cave. A little old man with a beard came out wearing cork shoes,” Pantoja told Manila in an interview, describing an initiation into a wilderness existence. “There were howling wolves, foxes, mountain goats, deer, scorpions, snakes. At night, I heard these animals and I was afraid.” The herder cared for Pantoja, keeping him warm with animal skins, teaching him to milk the goats, and how to hunt rabbits with a stick. Under the old man’s tutelage, Pantoja learned “the law of the jungle,” Manila wrote in his study. He understood he was different – “especially because he had hands” – but still felt part of their community, Manila wrote. He mastered animal sounds, from birdsong to the cry of the deer, and believed he could communicate “effortlessly with foxes, wolves and even snakes.” When the herder disappeared unexpectedly, Pantoja drew on the skills he had learned to survive on his own and gained the trust of a wolf pack by bringing food for their cubs and howling when he sensed danger. “I was crying and they jumped up at me… then they showed me the way to their cave, the wolf’s den,” Pantoja told Manila, describing the pups playing and jumping around as they greeted him. Pantoja avoided civilization, hiding whenever he heard human voices, until the Civil Guard found him, aged 19, “lost and alone, among the ravines,” Manila wrote. “I was doing very well and I didn’t know what money was but I never lacked food,” Pantoja told RTVE news show Informe Semanal in 2010. “If I wanted to fish, I fished in the river. If I wanted a rabbit, I caught it. If I wanted a deer, I called to my parents who were the wolves. I let out a howl, I hid in the river and the wolves brought the cattle down to me.” Returning to society Those who met Pantoja during the first months of his reintegration into society recalled his intelligence of nature and his “wild character,” Manila wrote in his study. The scholar noted his “complete lack of awareness when it came to social life, his language difficulties – especially his lack of knowledge of the names of things – his strange gait, his naiveté.” After being caught by the Guardia Civil in 1965, Pantoja lived with a priest in the southern city of Jaén, and with nuns in the capital Madrid. After completing his military service he ended up in Mallorca working in hotels and restaurants, RTVE said in a 2010 report. While on the Balearic island he had a chance encounter with anthropologist Manila, who studied his journey and became the first person to believe him, RTVE said. In his later years, Pantoja dedicated himself to sharing his story, “with the intention of protecting nature and fostering a better understanding of it,” his friend Arcones told RTVE. His life continued to draw interest, with Manila publishing his doctoral thesis as a book, “I played with Wolves,” and the release of a film adaptation of his life, “Among Wolves.” Pantoja built a new life in Rante, sharing a home with a retired police officer, according to a tribute from the local government posted Monday on social media. Later, a fellow resident gave him a house, and neighbors supported him, especially during his final two years of illness. “Marcos arrived in Rante with a story that the world knew,” the tribute read. “He leaves, leaving here a story that is also ours.”

articles.title: Screwworm is squeezing ranchers on both sides of the border
articles.summary: On Monday, the US government will reopen part of the southern border to Mexican livestock following a screwworm outbreak. It has reignited a decades-old debate in the cattle industry.
articles.body: Cattle rancher Johnny Mestas doesn’t want to get too worked up about New World screwworm, a fly whose parasitic larvae can eat cattle alive. The 74-year-old says he’s already had two heart attacks over the long course of his career farming in the parched San Luis Valley of southern Colorado. “Not everybody is meant to be a farmer,” said Mestas. “You’ve got to be half-crazy. There’s three elements you fight: the market, the weather and your neighbors.” Half-crazy or not, Mestas is uneasy about a new development in the ongoing saga of the screwworm: the US government’s plan to reopen part of the southern border to Mexican livestock on Monday. To prevent the spread of screwworm, the cattle trade with Mexico has been shuttered on and off since November 2024, with the current border closure put in place in July 2025. But next week, the border will reopen in Douglas, Arizona for cattle from Sonora, Mexico. The issue has reanimated a decades-old debate over protectionism within the cattle industry. Several US cattle producers say they are being pitted against Mexican ranchers and American meatpackers amid soaring beef prices for US consumers. Mexican producers are optimistic that the border reopening might staunch over a year of financial bleeding. Alvaro Bustillos, the head of the rancher’s union in the Mexican state of Chihuahua, hopes that a successful reopening in Sonora might lead to renewed cross-border trade with his region. The border closure nearly killed his business. “I had to fire people,” Bustillos told CNN. “It took me years to build my team. It took me years to build relationships. This is not only about the cattle trade. This is about families bonded together.” But US ranchers warn that they’re bleeding, too. One of the loudest voices in the cattle world agitating against the border reopening is Bill Bullard, the CEO of R-CALF, a national association of independent cattle and sheep farmers. Bullard, a former rancher from South Dakota, speaks about screwworm as one element of a broader crisis facing American ranchers: namely, an influx of less expensive cattle and beef from Mexico. “In just over a generation’s time, we wiped out half (of) our cattle producers in this country,” said Bullard in an interview with CNN. “It’s because we have been growing our dependence on foreign sources, displacing our domestic production in the United States. It is a threat to national security.” US officials had chosen to open the border at Sonora due to the state’s high industry standards and its lack of screwworm cases. Yet just days before, Sonora reported its first screwworm infestation, though the single case doesn’t appear to have slowed the US Department of Agriculture’s plans. The agency said Thursday that it intends to move ahead with the reopening. Even before Sonora reported its first case, many American ranchers like Mestas have been skittish about reopening the border, and not just because they worry screwworm could hitch a ride on Mexican cattle. US ranchers who don’t rely on Mexican cattle worry that bringing foreign livestock into the country could lower cattle prices, currently at historic highs. American consumers have been struggling with soaring beef prices for over two years now, but the elevated cost of livestock has been a relief for those ranchers, who feel they’re finally being paid fairly for their work. “These past few years, I actually made money!” Mestas said, with an audible hint of amazement. “Years and years, it was basically always break-even.” Beef prices, along with the broader cost of living, are also a salient political issue ahead of the 2026 midterms. Jenna Stanton, director of policy with the US Cattlemen’s Association (USCA), told CNN that many ranchers see the Trump administration’s push to open the border as an attempt to ease market pressures and lower the cost of beef. The White House had previously angered US ranchers by quadrupling low-tariff imports of Argentine beef to cool prices. On Friday, the president announced that the US would import 300,000 metric tons of beef to “reduce prices for Americans while giving space for our Great American Beef Herd to grow again.” The decision quickly drew criticism from cattle industry organizations. “There’s a midterm to be won this fall that, frankly, they are losing,” said Stanton. “They are looking to pull any lever they can.” CNN asked USDA about whether beef prices and the upcoming midterm elections had any bearing on the decision to reopen the Douglas port. The agency responded by sending CNN an op-ed by Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins that mentioned neither the elections nor beef prices. “If at any point we determine there is an imminent threat to our domestic herd, we will not hesitate to immediately pause the reopenings,” Rollins wrote. “Protecting American livestock will always come first, and we will continue using every tool at our disposal to support the ranchers who raise them and to eliminate (screwworm) once and for all.” Cries for economic protectionism by some ranchers and crises of animal health like screwworm often go hand-in-hand, according to agricultural historian Bill Winders of Georgia Tech. Bullard’s organization R-CALF similarly argued for a border closure with Canada during an outbreak of mad cow disease, a fatal brain-destroying condition, among Canadian livestock in the early 2000s. That closure lasted over two years. “These kinds of moments are often seized upon by organizations interested in protectionism,” said Winders. “And it can often help their position, even if just in the short term.” Winders notes that R-CALF only represents one part of the larger cattle supply chain. Numerous other agricultural organizations are in favor of the phased reopening, such as the National Cattlemen’s Beef Association (NCBA), a trade association for ranchers and feeders, including many who rely on Mexican livestock. The NCBA didn’t respond to multiple CNN requests for comment, but said in a statement posted online that the border reopening will “help normalize business for cattle operations throughout the border states and Southern Plains.” A ‘destroyed’ market Derrell Peel, a professor of agricultural economics at Oklahoma State University, is skeptical of R-CALF’s narrative about the benefits of border closures for the US cattle industry. Peel, who is an expert on the Mexican cattle trade, told CNN that screwworm isn’t the primary force behind high cattle prices, and sees the issue as a fig-leaf for a broader anti-free trade agenda. The high prices are due to the US cattle herd – the total population of cattle and calves in the US – being at a 75 year low after years of frequent, severe droughts, he said. That lack of supply, not just the screwworm, has pushed prices up. “We would have had record cattle prices (in the US) with or without the border closed,” Peel said. In the meantime, Peel added, Mexican ranchers have lost up to a thousand dollars per animal since the border closed to the livestock trade. One of those ranchers is Bustillos, the union head in Chihuahua, who declined to put a dollar figure on the money he’s lost to the border closure. “I lost a bunch of money,” Bustillos said. Closing the border to the cattle trade “destroyed the dynamics of the market.” He also worries about his colleagues in the US meatpacking industry, many of whom relied on Mexican exports to make their bottom line. Cattle that might have come to the US and fattened on American corn to be turned into steaks are now fed, slaughtered and packed entirely in Mexico – then sent to the US as boxed beef. According to USDA data, Mexico has exported 22% more boxed beef to the US this year. US meatpackers are responding with cutbacks. Last week, major meatpacking company Tyson Foods announced it is closing plants in Illinois and Utah and seeking to sell a facility in Washington, citing “one of the most historic cattle shortages the country has ever experienced.” “These cattle (in Mexico) had to go somewhere,” Bustillos said, “What the US doesn’t understand is they’re going to give all that leverage to Mexico as an industry.” Mexico has built out its ability to export beef significantly over the years, said Peel. He warns that the border closure’s disruption could last a long time. “The fact that (Mexico is now) absorbing those exportable cattle that they have not been exporting will probably lead to changes in the supply chain,” said Peel, “It might become more permanent in nature.” As for the animal health risk, many proponents point out that screwworm made it into the US either through infested wildlife or via flies themselves while the border was closed to the cattle trade. Sam Garcia, a Mexican American rancher and scientist who raises cattle in Sonora, told CNN that any livestock entering the US will be inspected numerous times for screwworm before being dipped in a chemical bath. Bleeding ranchers While expensive cattle may have given some American cattle producers breathing room, ranchers who spoke with CNN emphasized that high prices haven’t ensured easy wealth. Ranching is still difficult and often unprofitable work, especially for family operations. “Can we stop the bleed of the American rancher?” asks Cooper Little, the director of the Independent Cattleman’s Association of Texas. It’s a question he says he often poses when speaking with the thousands of small cattle ranchers in his organization, many of whom are elderly and struggling to stay afloat despite better revenue from high prices. Little, who speaks with an unmistakable Texas twang, saw the border closure as a chance to reshore the US cattle industry and stop the bleed. Without competition from Mexican producers, people might “have an interest in entering the beef cattle industry and being the legacy of their father or grandfather.” “It’s a hard life,” Little says of ranching. “And it’s getting harder every year.” J Storme Birdwell, who runs her family’s ranch on the Texas Gulf Coast, says day-to-day cattle production is a struggle. As expensive as cattle are, land is worth more. In recent years, Birdwell says she’s had trouble retaining leased plots of pastureland as younger generations of ranching families choose to cash out and sell rather than stay in the harsh world of agriculture. Those struggles are also intimately familiar to Mexican ranchers. Garcia, the Mexican American who raises cattle in Sonora, emphasizes that US and Mexican cattle producers are more similar than they are different, despite competing interests. “I can tell you,” Garcia said. “I have more in common with an American rancher than a politician in New York.” “The difference is labor might be cheaper down in Mexico, but also there’s not that many government incentives to be more productive” compared to the US, he said. Another of those shared issues is the lack of water. Ten years ago, Johnny Mestas in Colorado says he nearly lost his herd due to an expensive fight over water rights. Drought is an insidious threat to ranching life, and it’s only getting worse with climate change. “Some of my neighbors think I’m one rich sucker,” Mestas said, “But they don’t know half the sh–t we went through.”

articles.title: The trains that allow you to fall asleep in one world and wake up in another
articles.summary: In our roundup of travel stories this week: a teenager trapped by a collapsing sandcastle, the Vatican Observatory where science meets religion, plus “invisible architecture” in the African desert.
articles.body: In our roundup of travel stories this week: A collapsing sandcastle that trapped a teenager, the Vatican Observatory where science meets religion, plus “invisible architecture” in the African desert. Sleeper trains Few transport options capture romantic imaginations as completely as sleeper trains, those legendary locomotives that allow us to bed down in one world and wake up in another. For rail fans, there are overnight routes to discover on six of the world’s seven continents. They range from deluxe hotels on wheels ferrying guests to places such as Machu Picchu and the Taj Mahal, to the transcontinental giants of Canada and the USA with their spectacular “Vistadome” panorama cars. Here are 10 of our favorites. The release of the biopic “Tony” has renewed interest in superstar chef Anthony Bourdain. In 2014, he traveled to Russia on the eve of the Sochi Winter Olympic Games for CNN’s “Anthony Bourdain: Parts Unknown” and rode the luxury Grand Express sleeper train between Moscow and St. Petersburg. US-based subscribers can stream here. Grand designs The United Arab Emirates launched its first national passenger rail network earlier this summer, a long-awaited express train that criss-crosses the desert and will eventually connect 11 cities across the region. Emiratis are known for their love of cars, so introducing a rail system meant having to find a solution to getting people between the train stations and their homes or other destinations — all the more essential when summer temperatures in the country can hit more than 120 F (49 C). Farther south in the deserts of Namibia, so-called “invisible architecture” is on the rise. Upscale retreats are being designed to blend seamlessly into some of the African country’s most remote environments; being hard to find offers the ultimate in exclusivity. Where sacred meets celestial Science meets religion in the Vatican Observatory, a centuries-old center of astronomical research. Watch here as Reverend Richard D’Souza explains how his team studies meteorites and continues the search for extraterrestrial life. Completed just a few decades after the Vatican Observatory, in 1616, Istanbul’s Sultan Ahmed Mosque is one the world’s greatest sacred masterpieces. Popularly known as the Blue Mosque, it earns its moniker from the more than 20,000 Iznik tiles that decorate its interior’s upper reaches, meaning this is one place in the city where the heavens always glow a celestial blue. ‘50-year overnight success story’ Continuing our countdown of America’s Best Towns to Visit in 2026, we have Greenville, South Carolina, at No.3. For nearly 40 years, the magnificent urban waterfall that sits at the heart of Greenville’s downtown was covered over by a four-lane highway bridge. Imagination and determination was needed to redesign the town as it is today, with a vibrant energy that other cities crave and an extensive pedestrian and bike trail that links neighborhoods and attractions. Take a look, too, at the rest of our list so far: Roanoke, Virginia, at No. 10, Lawrence, Kansas, at No. 9, Iowa City, Iowa at No. 8, Juneau, Alaska, at No. 7, Burlington, Vermont, at No. 6, Fort Collins, Colorado, at No. 5 and Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, at No. 4. In case you missed it A teenager building a sandcastle was trapped after the hole caved in around him. The rescue operation took more than an hour. Watch here. A person was fined $5,000 for using a foghorn to wake a sleeping polar bear. Disturbing polar bears unnecessarily is illegal in Norway. A landmark trial. A sprawling hurricane. A royal relocation. What do you remember from the week that was? The Michelin Guide has awarded stars to restaurants for 100 years. These dishes tell its story.

articles.title: South Africa’s former world boxing champion Tete shot dead outside his home
articles.summary: Former world boxing champion Zolani “Last Born” Tete was shot dead outside his ​home in South Africa’s Eastern Cape province ‌on Friday, police and the country’s sports minister said.
articles.body: Former world boxing champion Zolani “Last Born” Tete was shot dead outside his ​home in South Africa’s Eastern Cape province ‌on Friday, police and the country’s sports minister said. The 38-year-old was arriving at his residence in Mdantsane township when ​two armed men wearing balaclavas got out ​of a vehicle and opened fire. “I will not ⁠speculate about who did this or why,” ​Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie said in a statement. Tete’s killing ​will renew attention on violent crime in South Africa, which continues to have one of the world’s highest murder rates ​despite recent declines in homicides. The murder ​of the world champion has also struck a chord in Mdantsane, ‌the ⁠Eastern Cape township that has produced some of South Africa’s most successful boxers. A 27-year-old woman travelling with Tete was shot multiple times and taken ​to hospital. Police ​have started ⁠investigations and the motive remains unclear. Tete won the IBF junior-bantamweight world title ​in 2014 after defeating Japan’s Teiru Kinoshita ​in ⁠Kobe. He later won the WBO bantamweight crown. He is best remembered internationally for his 11-second knockout of ⁠fellow ​South African Siboniso Gonya in ​Belfast in November 2017, the fastest stoppage in a world title ​fight.

articles.title: Move over, Usain Bolt: Humanoid robots smash human records at Beijing games
articles.summary: BEIJING — Chinese humanoid robots broke records set by humans, including beating Usain Bolt’s 100-meter sprint world record, on the opening day of the Olympics-like World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday.
articles.body: BEIJING — Chinese humanoid robots broke records set by humans, including beating Usain Bolt’s 100-meter sprint world record, on the opening day of the Olympics-like World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday. More than 2,000 humanoid robots were participating in the event, the organizer said. The five-day games, now in its second year, are a spectacle demonstrating China’s rapid progress in advanced robotics as the technology race with the U.S. heats up, with 51 events and more than 1,000 competitions taking place including running, table tennis and soccer. The games, which are taking place in the National Speed Skating Oval built for the 2022 Winter Olympics, opened the same week as Beijing held the 2026 World Robot Conference, where companies showcased around 3,000 products, including humanoid robots. China makes the majority of the world’s humanoid robots. The U.S. has stepped up scrutiny of robots from the country. Last month, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission announced a ban on imports of new foreign-made humanoid robots. The FCC cited national security reasons in a move that targeted China. The Pentagon recently also added Unitree, one of China’s leading humanoid robot makers, to its list of companies that it deemed have ties with the Chinese military. Beijing has hit back at the accusations. At Saturday’s opening of the robot games, the organizer and robot makers said that Chinese humanoid robots defeated human world records, as hundreds of humanoid robots marched in formation onto the field in a massive display of synchronized coordination. At a 100-meter sprint, a humanoid robot achieved a result of 9.39 seconds, beating the human record of 9.58 seconds set by Jamaican athlete Bolt in 2009. In a standing high jump, a humanoid robot was able to reach 2.88 meters, well above the 0.95 meters best result by a humanoid in last year’s first edition of the games. It surpassed the human high jump record of 2.45 meters set by Cuba’s Javier Sotomayor in 1993. Both robots were from Beijing-based X-Humanoid. Before the opening, a humanoid robot from Chinese smartphone company Honor completed a 100-meter sprint in a record of 9.32 seconds during a trial of the games, the company said, at a peak speed of 14.5 meters per second. Still, experts say humanoid robots are still mostly used for demonstrations, performances and research — at least for now — and it will still take time to achieve mass real-world deployment. Some spectators at the robot games said they were excited about the humanoid robots’ quickly improving abilities. Humanoid robots are “evolving rapidly,” said Li Yanfeng, an education worker and a Beijing resident. “At first, I wasn’t very accepting of artificial intelligence. I was even a bit resistant to it, because of the possibility that it might replace or displace humans,” she said. “But now that I see this development is unstoppable, I decided to come and take a look.” “These sports are perfectly normal for humans, but now robots can do them. I find it amazing,” said Yang Shangzheng, another spectator. Liu Tao, who was watching the games with his son, said that he was hoping to see “the best robots China currently has to offer.” This year’s robot games — which the organizer said has 16 countries participating, among them Germany, Japan and the U.S. — also include other events such as weightlifting and tug of war.

At Saturday’s opening of the robot games, the organizer and robot makers said that Chinese humanoid robots defeated human world records, as hundreds of humanoid robots marched in formation onto the field in a massive display of synchronized coordination. At a 100-meter sprint, a humanoid robot achieved a result of 9.39 seconds, beating the human record of 9.58 seconds set by Jamaican athlete Bolt in 2009. In a standing high jump, a humanoid robot was able to reach 2.88 meters, well above the 0.95 meters best result by a humanoid in last year’s first edition of the games. It surpassed the human high jump record of 2.45 meters set by Cuba’s Javier Sotomayor in 1993. Both robots were from Beijing-based X-Humanoid. Before the opening, a humanoid robot from Chinese smartphone company Honor completed a 100-meter sprint in a record of 9.32 seconds during a trial of the games, the company said, at a peak speed of 14.5 meters per second. Still, experts say humanoid robots are still mostly used for demonstrations, performances and research — at least for now — and it will still take time to achieve mass real-world deployment. Some spectators at the robot games said they were excited about the humanoid robots’ quickly improving abilities. Humanoid robots are “evolving rapidly,” said Li Yanfeng, an education worker and a Beijing resident. “At first, I wasn’t very accepting of artificial intelligence. I was even a bit resistant to it, because of the possibility that it might replace or displace humans,” she said. “But now that I see this development is unstoppable, I decided to come and take a look.” “These sports are perfectly normal for humans, but now robots can do them. I find it amazing,” said Yang Shangzheng, another spectator. Liu Tao, who was watching the games with his son, said that he was hoping to see “the best robots China currently has to offer.” This year’s robot games — which the organizer said has 16 countries participating, among them Germany, Japan and the U.S. — also include other events such as weightlifting and tug of war.

articles.title: Belgian car salesman becomes prince after DNA test proves royal parentage
articles.summary: A car salesman has formally become a prince at the age of 26 after being formally acknowledged as the son of the Belgian King’s brother Prince Laurent.
articles.body: A Belgian car salesman has become a prince at the age of 26 after being acknowledged as the son of the king’s brother, Prince Laurent. Clément Vandenkerckhove’s mother, a Belgian singer who had a relationship with Prince Laurent in the 1990s, only told him who his father was when he turned 16 a decade ago. It emerged this week that he was legally recognized as the son and heir of the 63-year-old younger brother of King Philippe, at a low-key town hall ceremony about six months ago after a DNA test proved his link to the royal family. Prince Laurent has registered his paternity of Vandenkerckhove with Belgium’s civil registry, The Telegraph reported on Wednesday. The formality affords the new prince equal inheritance rights to Laurent’s private estate with his half-sister Princess Louise, 20, and half-brothers Prince Nicolas, 20, and Prince Aymeric, 19, children Laurent shares with Princess Claire whom he married in 2003. But he will not receive a royal allowance, nor will he be expected to take on official duties, and he has no rights to the Belgian throne. Vandenkerckhove could take his father’s family name, Saxe-Coburg, but has indicated he may not choose to. “I am proud of the name Vandenkerckhove,” he recently told Flemish daily newspaper Het Nieuwsblad. “If I were to sacrifice that family name, it would be a betrayal of everything my mother has done for me.” Vandenkerckhove was born in August 2000 to Belgian singer Wendy Van Wanten, whose real name is Iris Vandenkerckhove. She and Laurent dated in the 1990s after a chance encounter at a fashion show in Paris but the relationship did not last and there has been speculation that Laurent’s father, the former king, disapproved. In a documentary that aired on Belgian network VTM last September, Vandenkerckhove recounted his mother’s admission that Laurent was his father. Four years after that, he contacted his father to share what he’d been told and Prince Laurent agreed to a DNA test. “We went to the hospital together and I remember him saying, ‘I’ll go first so you’re feeling at ease,’” Vandenkerckhove told VTM. Once paternity was confirmed, Vandenkerckhove said he and his father had engaged in “open and honest conversations.” This is not the first time a secret involving Belgium’s Royal Family has emerged. Laurent’s father, now 92, fought a paternity battle for many years before admitting in 2020 that he had fathered a daughter during an affair. Delphine Boël, 58, eventually won her legal fight and was granted the title of princess. She now uses the name Delphine de Saxe-Coburg.

articles.title: From fondue to casseroles: Classic 1960s foods that defined a generation
articles.summary: From fondue at the 1964 World's Fair to Julia Child's "The French Chef," these midcentury dishes defined American home cooking in the 1960s and '70s.
articles.body: The 1960s marked a shift in American cuisine as international dishes gained popularity, while the processed and convenience foods of the 1950s remained staples on dinner tables. C. A. Swanson & Sons introduced the frozen TV dinner in 1954, "marketing it as an easy-to-prepare, fun-to-eat meal, with a disposable tray that reduced cleanup time," the Smithsonian National Museum of American History reported. "The portable TV dinner tapped into middle-class Americans' excitement over television, allowing families to eat in front of their new sets." VINTAGE PHOTOS REVEAL WHAT GROCERY SHOPPING LOOKED LIKE IN THE 1960s Julia Child's first television cooking show, "The French Chef," debuted in 1963, and with it came a new approach to preparing foreign fare for middle-class home cooks. Do you remember eating the following classic dishes during the midcentury? Fondue The Swiss tradition of fondue took America by storm in the 1960s and ‘70s, thanks in part to the Swiss Pavilion serving Swiss cheese fondue at the 1964 New York World's Fair. Fondue is derived from the French word fondre, which means "to melt."  The dish involves melting cheese, wine and seasonings together in a pot and eating it communally with bread, meat and other items. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Fondue sets became a fashionable centerpiece of entertaining during the '60s and '70s. Casseroles As convenience cooking grew in popularity during the midcentury, casseroles incorporating canned and processed products fit the bill. Green bean casserole was created by Campbell's test kitchen employee Dorcas Reilly in 1955 and was originally called "Green Bean Bake," according to the company's website. "To this day, the recipe calls for only six ingredients: canned or fresh green beans, Campbell's Cream of Mushroom soup, soy sauce, black pepper, milk and French-fried onions," the website says. A recipe for tuna, noodle and mushroom soup casserole was included in the 1951 version of "The Joy of Cooking." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Chicken divan, a casserole combining chicken and broccoli in a creamy sauce and often topped with cheese and breadcrumbs, was another popular dish of the era. Chicken Kiev The exact origins of chicken Kiev are disputed, but it has connections to French culinary techniques and Eastern European cuisine, Tasting Table reported.  It is made by stuffing a chicken breast with cold, garlic-and-herb butter, breading the chicken and frying it. Frozen versions of this item are available in grocery stores today. French Onion Dip Lipton's introduced its dehydrated onion soup in the early 1950s.  By the middle of the decade, home cooks were combining it with sour cream to make what became known as California dip, later called French onion dip, a go-to snack item and party food, according to the website Quaint Cooking. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The dip has evolved from the original, two-ingredient recipe.  Modern iterations of it involve using Greek yogurt, whipped cottage cheese or cream cheese. Other retro food favorites that baby boomers may remember fondly include Swedish meatballs, chicken à la king and grasshopper pie. Swedish meatballs are typically made with a meat mixture, breadcrumbs and egg and topped with gravy. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Chicken à la king uses chicken, vegetables and a cream sauce and is typically served over toast, rice or noodles. Grasshopper pie is a no-bake dessert that incorporates crème de menthe and crème de cacao in a cookie crust.

articles.title: Iranian women defy efforts by hardliners to enforce wearing of hijab
articles.summary: A cultural faultline in Iran has re-emerged in recent months amid the turmoil of war and the revamping of the country’s hardline leadership: how and whether to enforce the wearing of the hijab by women.
articles.body: A cultural fault line in Iran has re-emerged in recent months amid the turmoil of war and the revamping of the country’s hardline leadership: how and whether to enforce the wearing of the hijab by women. At the height of the conflict with the United States this year, women without the headscarf were often seen at pro-government gatherings and in state media. The government and internal security forces had bigger issues to deal with. In one video an unveiled woman carrying an Iranian flag said her husband was in the military, and that she was proud of him. But in recent weeks, the clamor for restoring a hard line on what conservative clerics and politicians call “public nudity” has grown. Many Iranian women are openly flouting the rule – and authorities seem wary of launching a crackdown, for now. The regime appears to have more pressing priorities – presenting the conflict with the United States as an existential struggle, managing the deep economic fall-out and reorganizing the security apparatus under the leadership of Mojtaba Khamenei. Still, state media have been highlighting stories about cafes and other businesses being forced to close for failing to enforce rules on clothing. A CNN tally of articles in Iranian media at the end of last month found examples in half a dozen cities, including Tehran. Four years ago, the protest movement “Woman Life Freedom” ignited after the death in police custody of Mahsa Amini, a young woman who had been detained on accusations she was improperly dressed. It was brutally suppressed. Amnesty International reported at the end of 2024 that the Iranian authorities were waging war on women and girls “through an increasingly violent crackdown on those defying draconian compulsory veiling laws.” But the protests had lasting consequences. Despite the drumbeat of warnings and sporadic enforcement, there is widespread defiance of official regulations, especially among young Iranian women. On July 19, at least seven cafes and restaurants in Tehran were closed down for not enforcing the mandatory hijab, according to human rights group HRANA. The group also compiled lists of social media accounts that have been blocked for defying public dress codes. HRANA said authorities were using vague concepts such as “violation of norms,” “violation of modesty” and “failure to observe Islamic decency” in pursuing alleged offenders. But in one instance this month, it said a boutique was closed “due to unveiling,” without giving further details. On Monday the Tehran Prosecutor’s office said it would take serious action against alleged “indecency” violations and offenses at certain cafes and restaurants in Tehran, as well as shops selling clothing deemed “unconventional” or inappropriate. In the South Khorasan Province in eastern Iran, 10 cafes have been closed over alleged violations of “social norms and mandatory hijab rules,” the Mehr news agency reported, citing the province’s chief prosecutor. The relentless state media campaign on the issue often cites prayer leaders who insist the hijab is part of Iranian cultural identity and that women should observe modesty. Mohammad Javad Haj Ali Akbari, who leads Friday prayers in Tehran, claimed there were organized efforts to promote “nudity” and that some people are paid to appear in public with “improper” dress. There have been some high-profile cases. In June a popular Iranian singer, Parastoo Ahmadi, together with eight members of her band and production team, were sentenced in Qom to 74 lashes and banned from leaving the country for two years. Ahmadi had appeared with bare shoulders and uncovered hair at an event that she livestreamed on her YouTube channel in 2024. The charges included “offending public decency through the production and publication of vulgar and immoral content on cyberspace platforms.” Hardliners are stepping up pressure on the authorities. The editor of the journal Kayhan, Hossein Shariatmadari, wrote that enforcement is both a legal obligation and a religious duty for officials. A television show – “Park Way” – produced for the Tehran Municipality has devoted several episodes to the issue of women’s dress, calling for action against those who flout approved dress codes. One said that “unconventional behaviors should not be exhibited by anyone in public places such as parks.” Women have also been mobilized to demand the hijab be worn. At a small rally in Isfahan this week, one placard read: “Netanyahu: Unveiled women are our soldiers for free.” Netanyahu is not on record as making that remark, but the slogan reflects a broader narrative promoted by Iranian hardliners, portraying women who do not wear the hijab as, at the very least, disloyal to their country. But there’s plenty of evidence that many Iranian women are not intimidated by official campaigns. Social media videos have popped up showing young women on scooters wearing helmets, but no headscarves. The government is yet to fulfil a promise that women will be issued licenses to ride motorbikes. The videos include convoys of young women on scooters riding through Tehran and other cities. One Instagram post features a group of women declaring: “We’re the motorcycle girls of Shiraz! Shiraz girls, let’s go!” Another Instagram account posted video of about 20 female motorcyclists in the central city of Isfahan, describing it as “the biggest female motorcycle event in Isfahan.” As with so many social and cultural issues in Iran, the wearing of the hijab seems to some a misplaced priority at a time of conflict and economic crisis. That appears to include President Masoud Pezeshkian. Referring to an interview with a conservative cleric, he said: “The cleric mentioned hijab… Well, there are neighborhoods, there are mosques – go and work on it there! Can you really change people’s behavior through laws?” Pezeshkian went on to say that his daughter sometimes disagreed with him. “Does it mean I should force her?!” he asked. “Changing behavior is a cultural matter; it’s about belief. You can’t create belief in people through force.” Former MP Gholamali Jafarzadeh Imanabadi argued officials should focus on inflation and livelihoods instead of the hijab. And an unofficial media outlet posted an article entitled: A Provocation to a War-Weary Public - What Is Behind the Return of Hijab Patrols and Business Closures? Iranian authorities first began urging women to wear the hijab after the 1979 revolution. Before that, the monarchy had promoted a more secular and westernized image of women. Article 638 of Iran’s Islamic Penal Code criminalizes women appearing in public without “Islamic hijab,” although it does not precisely define what that means. A much tougher law approved in 2024 would have introduced a broader system of escalating penalties and surveillance, but its implementation was halted following intervention by the Supreme National Security Council. This has antagonized hardliners. One member of Iran’s parliament, Mohammad-Taqi Naqdali, said this week: “We see what the state of nudity and public vice is like in our midst…Israel and America cannot destroy us, but this decay that has plagued our religious culture and is spreading nudity in a disastrous and widespread manner in society will.” But the regime is treading carefully – for now. “They still don’t dare say anything to people on the street. Girls in Tehran are out and about wearing crop tops, shorts, and all kinds of clothes, and headscarves are practically no longer a thing,” one Tehran woman in her 60s told CNN by phone. “I don’t think they can make these girls wear headscarves again. But then again, that’s also what we thought when the revolution happened. We never thought they would be able to force us to wear them, but in the end, they did.”

articles.title: US supplies most of the world’s plasma. No country depends on it more than China
articles.summary: The US supplies 70% of the world’s plasma. China’s heavy reliance on its biggest geopolitical rival for this critical ingredient leaves its patients vulnerable.
articles.body: As she watched the pale yellow liquid drip into her mother’s vein, Ge Lan felt the weight of every drop. Her mother, recovering from stomach cancer surgery, relied on daily infusions of human albumin to restore her blood protein levels. At about $46 for a 10-gram bottle, the imported blood product was the costliest medicine in her mother’s treatment. “I just hope (she) gets better soon,” the 44-year-old told CNN. “I’m worried about the money too, but I have no choice.” Over two months, her mother used 72 bottles, costing the equivalent of seven months’ income for Ge, a local store worker in Henan, central China. Without help from her sister, she said she simply couldn’t have afforded the treatment – and without it, her mother’s condition could worsen. China is the world’s biggest consumer of human albumin, the most abundant protein in plasma, which is widely used in care for critical trauma such as burns, and restoring blood protein levels from chronic conditions, like liver diseases. But it’s long suffered a domestic shortfall largely due to strict rules on plasma collection – a legacy of an HIV infection scandal in the 1990s – and it remains heavily reliant on plasma from its biggest geopolitical rival, the United States, for much of its human albumin supply. The US supplies about 70% of global plasma and is one of the few countries that pays donors. Every year, millions of Americans offer up their arms to cover everyday costs – people like 25-year-old Sky Tucker. “While I do know it could save a life, most of the time, I’m just worried about if I’m gonna get my next meal or if I can feed my cats,” said the community college student who sold plasma twice a week for seven years to help make ends meet. More than 60% of China’s albumin market is supplied by foreign manufacturers and all of it is made from plasma collected in the US, according to a 2024 study co-authored by researchers from China’s national and Zhejiang drug inspection authorities. That reliance carries growing risks for Chinese patients. Researchers told CNN that China’s domestic plasma shortfall could leave patients vulnerable to drug shortages and price spikes if US-dominated supply flows are disrupted by geopolitical tensions or global health emergencies, like the Covid-19 pandemic. Beijing appears increasingly aware of that vulnerability. “That’s why they wanted to enhance the capacity of collecting the plasma in the Chinese market,” said Xi Chen, associate professor of Public Health at Yale University. After opening dozens of new licensed plasma collection centers in 2023, the country cleared its first rice-based albumin for market last July, as part of a broader push to reduce reliance on American plasma. Totally weaning itself off American plasma is deeply complicated for a country still haunted by a 1990s “plasma economy” scandal, where unsafe blood and plasma collection infected tens of thousands of rural residents in central China with HIV. The plasma scandal In the 1990s, local authorities in the impoverished Henan province pinned its economic ambitions on the plasma trade, rallying hundreds of thousands of cash-strapped farmers to sell their plasma, according to archived Chinese state media reports. “Stretch your arm, show your veins; one stretch, one fist — 50 yuan earned,” went the slogan spread widely through villages in central China, according to a 2004 report by The Beijing News, a state-run newspaper. Back then, 50 yuan was roughly equivalent to a month’s income for many rural residents. The frenzy followed Beijing’s decision in the mid-1980s to ban imports of almost all blood products – except human albumin – amid growing fears over the global HIV/AIDS crisis. China sought to build its own plasma-based industry – but the boom ended in catastrophe. The plasma collection spree, found to be rife with unsafe and unsanitary practices such as reused needles, ended up fueling one of China’s worst HIV outbreaks. Henan reported its first HIV case in 1995, prompting local authorities to shut down blood banks across the province. Nine years later, Henan officials admitted 25,000 former plasma sellers in the province had contracted HIV, according to a 2004 official provincial census reported by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV. Independent investigators, including the late doctor and whistleblower Gao Yaojie, argued the actual number could be much higher. It also left a lasting legacy of public distrust. The stigma from the past scandal still colors public perceptions of plasma donation as “dangerous” today, despite significantly improved safety and regulatory standards, according to a veteran industry executive in China, who talked to CNN on condition of anonymity as they weren’t authorized to speak publicly. Beyond reputational damage, Beijing’s tight regulatory grip over the past three decades – designed to prevent another blood contamination disaster – has also constrained manufacturers’ ability to produce lifesaving medicines, industry analysts say. This concern remained largely under the public radar until a Covid-era crunch thrust it into the spotlight. During the pandemic, plasma-based therapies like human albumin and intravenous immunoglobulin were widely used in treating critical Covid cases in China. A surge in demand then sparked a wave of panic buying, pushing up prices and leaving many patients with chronic conditions struggling to access supplies, according to a representative for a patient community impacted by inherited immune disorders. The person requested anonymity due to the sensitivity in speaking with foreign media. Since that time, calls for self-sufficiency in blood products have grown louder among industry stakeholders, academics, and political advisers – and efforts to address the plasma shortfalls have accelerated. After opening 32 new plasma collection centers in 2023, taking the total number to 302, China’s drug regulator approved the country’s first rice-derived recombinant human albumin, part of leader Xi Jinping’s broader push for China to seize the “commanding heights” in key technologies and industries. However, the rice-based albumin’s market adoption may be challenging, the veteran Chinese industry source believed, because it can only be used to treat liver cirrhosis – and the cost of production could be comparatively high. If China wants to increase its self-sufficiency, the source believes, the country needs to fundamentally update its decades-old regulatory regime. “China’s regulation of most other products has been getting closer and closer to international standards,” the source said. “But when it comes to blood products, regulation is still lagging far behind… It’s basically stuck at the level of the 1980s and 1990s.” Industry insiders say rules that restrict plasma collection centers to certain geographical areas, and only allow locally registered residents to donate, has left the world’s second-largest population with just 1.5 million to 3 million active plasma donors, according to estimates from Yale University’s Chen. By comparison, the US – with only a quarter of China’s population – has a larger pool of around 4 million, roughly estimated by Peter Jaworski, a professor at Georgetown University who studies the ethics and economics of the plasma business. The number of US plasma centers more than doubled from 601 in 2016 to more than 1,200 last year, according to historical data compiled by Jaworski, who leads the Georgetown Blood and Plasma Research Group. For comparison, that’s roughly the same number of Denny’s restaurants in the US and nearly double the number of Costco stores. The collection volume also jumped from over 35 million liters in 2015 to an estimated 62.5 million liters last year, according to Jaworski. “The industry is growing 6-8% every single year, and it doesn’t look like there’s anything to slow it down over the next 5 to 10 years,” Jaworski added, citing rising global demand for plasma-derived medicines. Most of the people who sell their plasma tend to be under 35, unemployed, without a college degree, Black and male, according to a 2021 study based on two proprietary national surveys conducted between 2018 and 2021. Whether the US paid-plasma industry exploits or alleviates financial hardship remains unsettled in public debate. China also pays plasma donors, but caps donations at every fortnight, up to 24 times a year – far fewer times than the US, where donors can roll up their sleeves up to twice a week, 104 times a year. The World Health Organization advocates for unpaid plasma collection for ethical reasons, arguing in part that it helps protect disadvantaged communities from possible coercion. However, Jaworski, who has donated plasma four times, says payment helps to ensure a sustainable supply of the raw material for lifesaving medicines. For Chinese patients – at least those who can afford the product – the question is less ethical than existential. Until China can produce or replace enough plasma of its own, tens of millions of patients needing human albumin, like Ge’s family, will remain heavily reliant on the vital fluid typically drawn from hard-up Americans. And that reliance begs an uncomfortable question for experts and the author McLaughlin: “If something happens in that country and that system needs to be shut down, where do you get the medication from?”

articles.title: Gas runs dry: Bangladesh factories shut, homes go dark
articles.summary: South Asia News: Bangladeshâs gas crisis has left the countryâs once-busy Ashuganj fertiliser factory silent for more than a year, disrupting fertiliser production, fo.
articles.body: Bangladeshâs gas crisis has left the countryâs once-busy Ashuganj fertiliser factory silent for more than a year, disrupting fertiliser production, forcing industries to cut output and contributing to power shortages and protests over fuel supplies.The state-owned factory, located near the eastern Titas gas field, shut down in March 2025 after a sharp decline in gas production, which was attributed to underinvestment in ageing fields and exploration. The crisis has since been compounded by disruptions to imports from the Middle East amid the US-Iran war.Ashuganj once operated around the clock, using natural gas to produce urea fertiliser for farmers across Bangladesh. The factory employed more than 1,200 people and produced more than 1,000 tonnes of fertiliser a day. It now stands largely idle, with machinery left unused.âOnly the skeleton of the factory remains,â said Md Bazlur Rashid, 59, who spent his entire working life at Ashuganj.âIt has lost its life," he added, as cited by AFP.Ashuganj is among six major urea fertiliser plants in Bangladesh that have either shut down or restricted operations because of gas shortages. Trade union leader Md Abu Kawsar said the shutdowns had cost workers their jobs while putting pressure on an industry closely linked to food security.âYou cannot simply let these factories sit idle and allow them to deteriorate,â Kawsar said. He added that reviving the plants could also help reduce pressure on the countryâs foreign currency reserves.The gas shortage has also spread across Bangladeshâs wider industrial sector. Hundreds of factories, including textile plants, have either reduced production or shut down, affecting an industry that accounts for about 80% of the countryâs export earnings and makes Bangladesh the worldâs second-largest garment exporter.Households have also faced disruptions, with domestic piped-gas supplies frequently cut. Gas-fired power plants are struggling to meet electricity demand, resulting in regular blackouts.The government introduced electricity-saving measures in August, including an order for shopping malls to close one hour earlier, as the gas shortage continued to strain the countryâs energy supply.Electricity generation, industrial units and captive power plants account for more than three-quarters of Bangladeshâs natural gas consumption, leaving households to bear the impact of worsening shortages.Households account for just over a tenth of the countryâs gas consumption but have also faced frequent disruptions. âWe don't get a drop of gas overnight,â said housewife Nargis Begum, 50, who lives near the Ashuganj factory.âThen sometimes the pressure is too low. We can't turn on two burners at the same time.âMany households, particularly in rural areas, have switched to wood-burning stoves, while frequent power cuts have left residents without fans amid sweltering humidity.âThere is no let-up in our suffering,â Begum said. âThere is no guarantee of electricity. It's so hot now. Last night, there were three or four outages.âThe shortages have also triggered protests among gas-powered rickshaw drivers, who have blocked roads after spending hours waiting for fuel.The crisis has been building for years. Bangladesh was largely self-sufficient in natural gas in 2018, but production declined as older fields were depleted while demand continued to rise. The country has increasingly relied on imports, with Qatar emerging as a key supplier.Experts have said successive governments failed to invest sufficiently in gas exploration. Energy Minister Iqbal Hasan Mahmud Tuku blamed the previous government of Sheikh Hasina, which was ousted in a 2024 revolution, for failing to drill new wells.âThe previous government stayed away from gas exploration,â he told an energy security conference in Dhaka in July. âOur dependence on imports has brought us to this point.âCatch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Man leaves tired 7-year-old son alone on Mount Fuji during family hike
articles.summary: A man who left his tired 7-year-old son to wait alone on Japan’s Mount Fuji while he continued a family hike has been reprimanded by police.
articles.body: A man who left his tired 7-year-old son to wait alone on Japan’s Mount Fuji while he continued a family hike has been reprimanded by police. The boy was spotted sitting on his own at a hut about 8,200 feet (2,500 meters) above sea level – slightly more than halfway up the country’s tallest mountain – by a worker on Thursday, according to CNN’s affiliate TV Asahi. The case was then reported to the police. Police said the boy had gone hiking with his father and older brother and was told to wait there when he became “tired” and reluctant to continue walking, TV Asahi reported. He was told to wait on a bench at the sixth station of the Fujinomiya trail as his father and brother continued their ascent, the report said. When they returned five hours later, police were waiting with the young boy, who was unharmed and handed back to his father. The officers warned the man he could be held criminally liable, the Japanese TV broadcaster reported, adding that he expressed his remorse. Climbers of the 12,388 feet-tall (3,776 meters) volcano have had to be rescued after suffering altitude sickness in the past. Weather conditions up the mountain can also be unpredictable. Authorities have introduced new rules in recent years, including a cap on the maximum number of climbers per day and requiring them to take a brief class about hiking safety.

articles.title: A tiny owl flew 70 miles out to sea and collapsed on a yacht, exhausted and too weak to fly, she found an unlikely group of rescuers who refused to leave her behind
articles.summary: Europe News: A British Army sailing crew got recently an unexpected passenger during a race around Britain and Ireland when an exhausted barn owl landed on their b.
articles.body: A British Army sailing crew got recently an unexpected passenger during a race around Britain and Ireland when an exhausted barn owl landed on their boat about 70 nautical miles from shore.The bird was found struggling in the open sea on Thursday while the crew of Fujitsu British Soldier was taking part in the 50th Anniversary RORC Round Britain and Ireland Race. According to Reuters, the sailors saw the owl fall into the water several times before it finally managed to reach the boat.The exhausted bird then collapsed on the deck. The crew secured it with a towel and began looking after it as they continued towards the finish line at Cowes. They later named the owl Little Reg, before changing the name to Little Regina.The Barn Owl Trust, Marine and Wildlife Rescue and Caister Independent Lifeboat also became involved in getting the bird safely back to shore while the Army Sailing Association crew continued the race.Owl kept trying to reach boatAccording to Sergeant Mark Petherbridge of 2nd Battalion, The Parachute Regiment, the bird tried to get onto the boat after falling from the mast and into the sea. "We thought we'd lost her, but she kept fighting her way back up and to the boat," Petherbridge said.The bird had reportedly tried to land on the head of one of the crew members before tumbling into the water. It fell into the sea three times before eventually making it onto the deck.Once aboard, the sailors realised that the owl was extremely tired. Skipper Will Naylor told race officials that the crew now had an additional member for the latter part of the race."We have an extra crew member for the latter parts of the race. An exhausted barn owl that we are nursing back to health," Naylor said. He also joked about the unusual addition to the crew, saying, "Someone is going to have to walk the plank!"The sailors continued to care for the owl as their boat made its way towards Cowes. The race covered 1,805 nautical miles, and the crew could not simply stop their journey to take the bird back to land.Wildlife groups pitch inAs the sailors continued their journey, arrangements were made to get the owl off the racing boat and back to land. The Barn Owl Trust, Marine and Wildlife Rescue and Caister Independent Lifeboat helped with the rescue. The lifeboat collected the bird so it could be taken to a wildlife centre for further care.The owl was eventually transferred to the RSPCA East Winch Wildlife Centre in King's Lynn, England. Staff at the centre said the bird was in poor condition when it arrived."The owl is sadly very emaciated and weak, but is now receiving fluids, nutrition, warmth and plenty of rest.
